title: Royal charter granted to the East India Company
summary: Elizabeth I granted a charter to the Company in late 1600. The British Library's archival description and some printed charter compilations differ on the day.

title: Battle of Plassey
summary: Company forces under Robert Clive defeat the Nawab of Bengal, Siraj ud-Daulah, aided by defections arranged with Mir Jafar, who became Nawab.

title: Company receives the diwani of Bengal
summary: In 1765 Mughal emperor Shah Alam II granted the Company diwani revenue-collection authority for Bengal, Bihar and Orissa; exact day is not asserted here.

title: Great Bengal famine
summary: Severe famine occurred in Bengal in 1770. The British Library catalogues parliamentary reports on the famine and revenue collection. Mortality and relative responsibility of climate, markets, and Company policies require detailed review.

title: Regulating Act
summary: Parliament enacted the Regulating Act amid the Company's financial crisis, changing governance and oversight. Day-level dating has not been established from the reviewed archival catalogue.

title: Company rule ends; Crown assumes control of India
summary: Following the 1857 rebellion, the Government of India Act transfers the Company's territories and armies to the Crown.

title: Iran nationalizes its oil industry
summary: Iran's oil nationalization legislation was adopted in spring 1951; the Shah promulgated an implementation law on May 1 while Mossadegh was prime minister.

title: Coup removes Mossadegh
summary: An August 19 coup overthrew Prime Minister Mohammad Mosaddegh. Declassified American records document CIA direction, British cooperation, and Iranian political participation; relative contributions remain debated.

title: Iranian oil consortium agreement signed
summary: Iran and an international oil consortium signed an agreement in September 1954; parliamentary and royal approvals followed in October. Iranian ownership and foreign operating rights were distinct.

title: CIA publicly acknowledges its role
summary: The National Security Archive published declassified CIA excerpts acknowledging the agency's planning and direction of the 1953 coup. This was not the first public disclosure of U.S. involvement.

title: Treaty of Paris settles major imperial fronts of the Seven Years' War
summary: Britain gained substantial territory, while wartime debt and new frontier governance problems complicated relations with North American colonies and Indigenous nations. British victories also occurred in India.

title: Pontiac's resistance challenges British frontier rule
summary: Indigenous communities resisted British control and settler encroachment in the Great Lakes and Ohio Valley; alliances and aims differed among communities.

title: Royal Proclamation restricts settlement beyond the Appalachians
summary: The British Crown sought to restrict colonial settlement beyond a proclamation boundary, challenging land speculation while Indigenous territories remained contested and settlement continued.

title: Parliament passes the Stamp Act
summary: Colonial revenue legislation proposed under Prime Minister George Grenville provoked protests and political mobilization in Britain's North American colonies.

title: Townshend duties renew colonial taxation disputes
summary: After the Stamp Act's repeal, Parliament introduced new import duties, including the tea duty that remained relevant to the protests of 1773.

title: Tea Act benefits the financially troubled East India Company
summary: Parliament eased the East India Company's tea sales into North American colonies without repealing the existing tea duty, alarming merchants and opponents of taxation without representation.

title: Boston protesters destroy East India Company tea
summary: A colonial protest group boarded three vessels carrying East India Company tea and destroyed the cargo after controversy over parliamentary taxation and monopoly privileges.

title: Parliament responds with Coercive Acts
summary: British legislation closed Boston's port and curtailed Massachusetts self-government in response to resistance and the destroyed East India Company tea.

title: First Continental Congress meets in Philadelphia
summary: Colonial delegates coordinated responses to British policy, culminating in an association calling for an economic boycott, amid disagreement over how far to resist.

title: Armed fighting begins at Lexington and Concord
summary: British regular troops and Massachusetts militia engaged in combat as royal authorities tried to seize colonial military supplies amid escalating disputes.

title: Bank of England record concerns extension of an East India Company loan
summary: An archival note to East India Company chairman Henry Crabb Boulton concerns prolonging an existing £50,000 Bank of England loan. The catalogue does not establish a new disbursement on this date.

title: East India Company faces a financial crisis
summary: Financial difficulties after Company expansion prompted British parliamentary investigation and government consideration of relief and oversight.

title: Parliament authorizes a loan for the East India Company
summary: Parliament addressed the Company's crisis through legislation permitting public financial assistance. An 1813 parliamentary review describes a £1.4 million government loan; payment terms and disbursement require direct statutory/account review.

title: Robert Clive defends his Bengal record before Parliament
summary: MP Robert Clive defended himself during several days of Commons debate over a committee investigation chaired by John Burgoyne into East India Company practices in India.

title: Boston tea consignee appointments become public
summary: The Boston Gazette identified Richard Clarke, Benjamin Faneuil and two sons of Governor Hutchinson among expected recipients of East India Company tea; consignments involved prospective commercial commissions.

title: Joshua Winslow privately describes anticipated tea commission
summary: Tea consignee Joshua Winslow wrote Jotham Gay about the Company's tea scheme, its price advantages and a potentially handsome commission; the letter does not establish that any commission was paid.

title: Boston tea consignees petition the governor and council
summary: Council records cited in a scholarly edition identify a November 19 petition from Richard Clarke, Benjamin Faneuil, Thomas Hutchinson Jr. and Elisha Hutchinson during the tea crisis.

title: East India Company's royal charter expands governing and military powers
summary: Charles II authorized the Company to govern its settlements, raise forces, coin money and act against unauthorized traders. British Library notes that Company lending to the Crown during 1660–1684 helped explain growth in privileges; do not treat this as a one-for-one purchase of specific powers.

title: Bank of England chartered to finance war with France
summary: Subscribers raised £1.2 million to fund a government loan at 8% interest, secured by specified taxation. A joint-stock bank was chartered; it was not yet the modern nationalized central bank.

title: Public borrowing arrangement establishes rival East India trading organizations
summary: A planned £2 million government borrowing program was coupled to East India trading privileges. The General Society and new English Company were chartered, while the old Company held a £315,000 stake in the new one; original subscriber and payment ledgers require follow-up.

title: Old and new East India companies unite under one corporation
summary: After a 1702 coalition and 1708 financial reconciliation, the old East India Company surrendered its charter in 1709 and the united corporation operated under the new company's 1698 legal charter.

title: South Sea Company founded around public-debt and trading privileges
summary: The South Sea Company was established in connection with restructuring British government debts and prospective Atlantic trade rights. The company later operated voyages involving enslaved Africans; traded people were not simply financial abstractions.

title: South Sea debt-conversion scheme prevails against competing Bank proposal
summary: The South Sea Company competed with the Bank of England to acquire government debt; a major debt-to-equity program was approved and Company stock prices rose sharply. Precise competing bid terms require the full archival documents.

title: South Sea share bubble collapses and political corruption is investigated
summary: After rapid appreciation, South Sea stock prices fell. A Bank archive historical note documents political bribery concerns, including Chancellor John Aislabie. Financial losses and longer-run national effects were uneven; narratives of universal ruin exaggerate the record.

title: Bank of England signs agreement to acquire South Sea Company stock
summary: A Bank of England archive catalogue describes the 23 October 1722 agreement for a stock purchase. A separate circa-1722 proposal discusses £4.2 million; the catalogue alone does not establish disbursement dates or executed cash transfers.

title: Weavers protest Indian cotton imports amid economic anxieties
summary: English silk and wool weavers protested imported Indian calico in London and other towns; some rioters assaulted women wearing calico. Distinct groups and participants had differing actions and demands.

title: East India, Bank and South Sea financial representatives discuss rescue
summary: The East India Company appointed a committee to meet representatives of the Bank of England and South Sea Company as liquidity tightened after the Bubble. Robert Walpole separately advocated an engraftment proposal, but his attendance at this committee meeting is not established here.

title: Calico restriction and South Sea Engraftment legislation gain royal assent
summary: Two laws became effective as legislation on the same date: one restricted Indian calico in Britain, the other authorized an approach to transferring South Sea Company debt onto Bank and East India Company books. Legal authorization alone did not constitute a transfer.

title: East India Company gains restrictions on rival imports into British colonies
summary: New legal rules strengthened East India Company access to imperial markets by restricting British colonial imports of East India goods routed through foreign European suppliers. A debated proposal to permit slave trading from Madagascar was not enacted.

title: Debt-engraftment authorization never produces planned transfers
summary: The 1721 Engraftment Act lacked compulsion, and neither the Bank of England nor the East India Company actually took over South Sea debt under its scheme. Subsequent plans and 1722 agreements must be investigated independently.

title: French Regency inherits large postwar financial liabilities
summary: After Louis XIV's death, the regent Philippe d'Orléans faced war-related debt and pressure to revive French commerce and colonial investment; this context helped attract John Law's monetary proposals.

title: John Law establishes Banque Générale
summary: Law founded a French bank issuing paper notes in 1716, with backing and permissions under the regency; the later Banque Royale phase was a distinct legal change.

title: Compagnie d'Occident assumes Louisiana monopoly privileges
summary: Law organized a colonial trading company and received French Louisiana trade privileges, linking projected colonial revenues with government-debt conversion ideas. Colonial territory was not uninhabited.

title: New Orleans is founded in French Louisiana
summary: Bienville selected the settlement site with assistance from Indigenous advisers. The city developed through coerced and indentured labor, including enslaved African builders.

title: French trading companies consolidate as Compagnie des Indes
summary: The colonial enterprise absorbed further trading companies and was consolidated under the name Compagnie des Indes, with subsequent state-associated minting and revenue privileges.

title: French state debt exchanged or targeted for Company stock
summary: Law promoted debt conversion through subscriptions to new Company shares. A New York Fed historical commentary describes a plan addressing 1.5 billion livres of public debt, but this target is not evidence that this entire amount was retired.

title: John Law becomes Controller General of French Finances
summary: The financier formally assumed senior fiscal office while associated banks and trading companies occupied central roles in public finance and colonial policy.

title: Mississippi Company and paper-note system collapse
summary: Stock price supports, monetary restrictions and speculative pressures failed; shares fell sharply, paper money lost credibility and Law's system unraveled. The relative responsibilities and long-term macroeconomic effects are historically debated.

title: John Law departs France after collapse
summary: John Law left France in December 1720 following financial collapse and political opposition. The French Company and Louisiana colony continued thereafter in altered form.
